section_summary: This section contains English summaries and translations of Japanese station JZK broadcasts from September and October 1941, accompanied by two FBI cover letters forwarding groups of transcripts to the State Department. The broadcasts report Japanese operations in China, the German campaign against the Soviet Union, and diplomatic developments, alongside commentaries promoting Japan’s Greater East Asia policy and criticizing British and American actions. Several transcripts note severe interference or poor recordings.

subfiles.title: JZK program transcript, date not shown
subfiles.about: News and commentary cover American naval escorts, lend-lease, developments in Asia, Manchoukuo, and Japanese women's wartime life.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages finish a news bulletin and summarize a commentary presenting Manchoukuo as proof of Japan's aims in East Asia. A talk by Eiko Fujikawa discusses women's wartime service and clothing; the station announces a revised broadcast schedule beginning September 24.

subfiles.title: JZK program, September 28, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports on Changsha, the Tripartite Pact anniversary, the Dutch East Indies, and the German–Soviet war.
subfiles.summary: News claims Japanese success at Changsha and summarizes anniversary broadcasts by Ambassadors Oshima and Horikiri. It also covers evacuees from the Dutch East Indies, American naval defense zones, and the Moscow aid talks. A recording of Information Bureau director Ito reaffirms Japan's Axis policy.

subfiles.title: JZK program, September 29, 1941
subfiles.about: News covers Japanese operations in China, Tripartite Pact ceremonies, the Moscow conference, and a weekly review.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin claims further Japanese advances and air raids in China and reports on German operations and American debate over neutrality. A weekly review revisits Changsha, the Tripartite Pact anniversary, wartime food measures, and domestic observances.

subfiles.title: JZK program, September 30, 1941
subfiles.about: A badly recorded program carries fragmentary news and commentary on China and the Moscow conference.
subfiles.summary: Poor reception left most news and the Hunan commentary unintelligible.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 5, 1941
subfiles.about: A noisy recording includes a historical story, fragmentary international news, and a commentary on Changsha.
subfiles.summary: Most news is indistinct; the commentary portrays the Changsha operation as weakening Chongqing.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 6, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast combines fragmentary war news with a weekly review of Japanese operations in China.
subfiles.summary: Poor reception permits only brief notes on China, the German–Soviet war, Manila talks, and wartime commemorations.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 7, 1941
subfiles.about: News and commentary address the China war, the German advance on Moscow, and Allied cooperation in East Asia.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary news covers fighting in China, Indochina–Thailand border demarcation, Afghanistan, and the German advance. A longer commentary argues that the Moscow conference and a British–American meeting in Manila form part of an anti-Japanese encirclement, while insisting Japan will establish its East Asian sphere.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 8, 1941
subfiles.about: The program discusses Japanese–American negotiations, aid to Chongqing, Japanese campaigns in China, and German operations.
subfiles.summary: Newspaper editorials warn that relations with America may deteriorate. Reports discuss Allied economic and military aid to Chongqing, Japanese operations in Hunan and elsewhere, and the German advance. The commentary claims three Japanese autumn campaigns have weakened Chongqing.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 9, 1941
subfiles.about: News covers Japanese personnel and resource planning, oil restrictions, and the German–Soviet war.
subfiles.summary: The broadcast reports Wakasugi's arrival in Washington, an Indochina resource survey, and an oil shipment ban. Despite worsening reception, its commentary criticizes British and American defense coordination and their advisers in Chongqing.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 10, 1941
subfiles.about: News and commentary cover China, German claims of Soviet defeats, American interests in China, and Panama's coup.
subfiles.summary: The program reports Japanese military and cultural activities in China and Indochina, then repeats German claims about Soviet losses and the drive on Moscow. It alleges an American plan to control Chinese mineral resources and reports Panama's change of government. The commentary depicts Chongqing as corrupt, hungry, and near collapse.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal of Tokyo broadcast transcripts, September 20–October 4
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The FBI forwards translated Tokyo radio broadcasts for September 20 through October 4, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards broadcast transcripts by special messenger.

subfiles.title: JZK program, September 20, 1941
subfiles.to: Radio audience, including children in Hawaii
subfiles.about: News and talks cover Japanese operations in China, the German–Soviet war, Manchoukuo, and Japanese aviation.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin reports Japanese claims from Hunan and other Chinese fronts, German gains in Ukraine, and Roosevelt's lend-lease request. A long commentary argues that Britain and America fear Soviet defeat and condemns their actions in Iran while predicting Turkey will favor Germany. A children's segment revisits Manchoukuo; Saburo Yamajiku discusses Japanese aviation.

subfiles.title: JZK program, September 22, 1941
subfiles.about: A poorly recorded broadcast reports on Japanese operations, German advances, and the week's domestic events.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary news covers fighting near Dongting Lake, Indochina, Kyiv, and the Atlantic war. The weekly review recalls the Manchurian Incident anniversary, air defense observances, and Admiral Shimada's appointment.

subfiles.title: JZK program, September 26, 1941
subfiles.about: News and a lengthy economic commentary address American neutrality, Pacific defense, and the freezing of Japanese assets.
subfiles.summary: The news reports French protests to Britain, American neutrality-law debate, naval construction, and Singapore. The commentary argues that British and American asset freezes have hurt Shanghai, Hong Kong, the Dutch East Indies, Burma, and the Philippines while strengthening Japan's trade with Indochina and Thailand. Domestic items follow.

subfiles.title: JZK program, September 27, 1941
subfiles.about: A noisy anniversary broadcast reports Changsha fighting and commemorates the Tripartite Pact.
subfiles.summary: The surviving notes summarize anniversary speeches and a commentary defending the pact.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 1, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast reports on China and the German–Soviet war and carries extended commentaries on Duff Cooper and Changsha.
subfiles.summary: News makes large claims of Japanese victories in Hunan and reports the Moscow aid conference and German operations. One commentary portrays Duff Cooper's East Asian mission as an effort to strengthen an anti-Japanese cordon. Wakao Oiwa then argues that Chongqing concealed Changsha's fall to preserve British and American confidence and aid.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 2, 1941
subfiles.about: Poorly received news and commentary cover Japanese operations and the three-power Moscow conference.
subfiles.summary: News includes Chinese diplomatic appointments, claims from the German front, and Allied aid pledges to the Soviet Union. The commentator argues that shipping and Soviet production problems will frustrate the pledged aid.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 3, 1941
subfiles.about: News covers Hunan, Japan's protest to Iran, German operations, and Iceland; commentary celebrates Japanese gains.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin gives Japanese casualty claims for Hunan, reports a diplomatic protest to Iran, and relays German war claims. Commentary portrays the Hunan operation as a decisive victory welcomed by Chinese civilians.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 4, 1941
subfiles.about: Fragmentary news and commentary concern Soviet supply shipping, Iran, Atlantic sinkings, and Duff Cooper.
subfiles.summary: Poor reception leaves only a brief account of commentary accusing Duff Cooper of strengthening an anti-Japanese encirclement.

subfiles.title: FBI transmittal of Tokyo broadcast transcripts, October 16–21
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The FBI forwards translated Tokyo radio broadcasts for October 16 through October 21, 1941.
subfiles.summary: Hoover encloses the next group of Tokyo broadcast transcripts.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 16, 1941
subfiles.about: The broadcast addresses Japanese–American tensions, the Soviet defense of Moscow, and Yasukuni Shrine observances.
subfiles.summary: Captain Hiraide warns of acute Pacific tensions, while an Asahi editorial urges America to reconsider its policy. Reports describe Soviet evacuation preparations, German advances, and Allied advisers in Chongqing. The commentary honors the dead at Yasukuni Shrine; regional domestic news follows.

subfiles.title: JZK program, October 17, 1941
subfiles.about: A severely disrupted recording reports the resignation of the third Konoe Cabinet.
subfiles.summary: The recorder stopped after brief, mostly inaudible news notes.
